problems.stem: A usability plan states a findability hypothesis but its only metric is a satisfaction rating. As a coherence reviewer, what is the core problem?
options: The metric cannot test the hypothesis: a satisfaction rating does not measure whether users can find the feature.
Satisfaction ratings are never allowed in a plan.
The hypothesis should have been removed.
problems.explanation: A coherent plan requires the metric to be able to confirm or disconfirm the stated hypothesis; satisfaction cannot test findability.

problems.stem: A plan's hypothesis targets first-time users, but the recruitment line says "5 expert designers," and the tasks list exact click steps. Which two parts are misaligned with the hypothesis?
options: The metric and the decision rule.
The participant sample (experts, not first-time users) and the tasks (leading click paths that hide findability).
Only the title and the references.
Nothing is misaligned; the plan is fine.
problems.explanation: Coherence means every part serves the hypothesis; an expert sample and leading tasks both undercut a first-time-user findability claim.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to generate a complete usability plan from a one-line brief. What is the defensible boundary on using the output?
options: Submit the generated plan as your studio artifact since it is complete.
Run the coherence audit yourself, checking that the AI's hypothesis, sample, tasks, metrics, and decision rule all trace to the same goal, and fix the mismatches.
Reject the AI plan entirely; plans must be hand-built end to end.
Use the AI plan only to make the wording sound more professional.
problems.explanation: A generated plan can look complete yet be internally incoherent; the designer must audit and reconcile its parts.

problems.stem: A plan's decision rule reads "ship if participants seem to like it." Even with a good hypothesis, sample, and tasks, why does this break the plan's coherence?
options: Decision rules are optional in a usability plan.
The decision rule does not connect to the plan's own metrics or thresholds, so the evidence the study gathers cannot actually drive the decision.
Liking a product is the strongest possible evidence.
The rule should have come before the hypothesis.
problems.explanation: A coherent plan ties the decision rule to the metrics and thresholds it collects; a vague rule disconnects evidence from the decision.
